questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet shows output rising while nutrition stays flat; is this growth or development?

options.text: It is growth, not development, since output rose without broader welfare gains.
It is development only, because nutrition is a welfare measure.
It is growth only, because output rose but living standards did not improve.
options.misconception: confuses any output rise with development

options.text: It is neither, because recipes are not national output.

questions.explanation: Growth means rising real output; development means broader welfare gains. Output rose here, so growth occurred without development. The tempting idea that welfare alone defines development ignores output.
questions.hint: Check whether output or welfare changed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet shows a lagging kitchen growing faster than the leader; what is this called?

options.text: Convergence failure, because leaders always stay ahead.
options.misconception: assumes leaders never lose relative ground

options.text: Catch-up growth, because poorer kitchens can grow faster by adopting known methods.
Diminishing returns, because extra capital yields less.
options.misconception: confuses a cause with the phenomenon itself

options.text: Steady state, because growth rates equalize instantly.

questions.explanation: Catch-up growth means poorer economies grow faster by adopting existing technology. The leader need not stay ahead forever. Diminishing returns is a mechanism, not the name.
questions.hint: Name the faster growth of laggards.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet budgets 20 percent of output saved; why does this raise future output?

answer.exemplar: Higher saving funds more investment in capital, which raises future productive capacity and output. The tempting view that saving merely hoards money ignores its investment channel.

questions.explanation: Saving becomes investment in capital, raising future capacity. Hoarding alone would not raise output. The channel from saving to investment is the key link.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet seeks the savings rate maximizing consumption; what condition defines it?

options.text: The savings rate equals the depreciation rate.
options.misconception: confuses steady state with golden rule

options.text: Consumption is zero at the golden rule.
The savings rate equals one minus the capital share.
The marginal product of capital equals the sum of depreciation and population growth.

questions.explanation: The golden rule holds when MPK equals depreciation plus population growth. Equalizing saving and depreciation only keeps capital per worker constant. Maximizing consumption requires the marginal condition.
questions.hint: Set MPK equal to break-even investment.

questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet compounds 5 percent for 6 years; growth factor?
questions.explanation: (1.05)^6 is about 1.34. Linear addition gives 1.30. Compounding raises the factor over several periods.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet uses a 14 percent rate; doubling time by the rule of seventy?
questions.explanation: 70 divided by 14 equals 5 years. Using 72 would give 5.14. The rule approximates doubling time for moderate rates.
